title: Ukrainian Borscht
subtitle: Hearty beetroot and cabbage soup with smoked pork
excerpt: A thick, deeply coloured beetroot soup with cabbage, potato, carrot, and smoked pork in a rich beef stock. Serve with a spoonful of soured cream and dark bread.
sourceNotes: Ukrainian borscht; thicker and more vegetable-laden than Russian versions. Smoked pork and beef stock are the traditional base. Vinegar is added to fix the red colour.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the soup without the soured cream. Cool completely, freeze in portions for up to 3 months. Reheat gently and add soured cream at serving.
recipe.batchNotes: Makes a large pot naturally. Keeps well in the fridge for up to 4 days and improves overnight.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best made a day ahead. The flavour deepens overnight. Reheat gently over a low heat, stirring often, as the soup can catch on the bottom.

content.text: Ukrainian borscht is a thick, hearty soup built on beetroot, cabbage, and potato in a meaty stock. The vinegar added at the end is not optional: it holds the deep red colour and gives the soup its characteristic sharpness. Add soured cream at the table, not while the pot is still on the heat.

Heat the oil in the frying pan over a medium heat. Cook the onion for 6 minutes until soft. Add the carrot and cook for another 4 minutes. Add the garlic and tomato puree and stir for 2 minutes. Set aside.
Pour the stock into the stockpot and bring to a simmer. Add the smoked pork sausage and bay leaves. Simmer for 15 minutes.
Add the potato and cabbage. Simmer for 10 minutes.
Add the grated beetroot, the onion and carrot mixture, and the tinned tomatoes. Stir well. Simmer for 25 minutes until all the vegetables are completely tender.
Add the cider vinegar and sugar. Taste and adjust with salt, pepper, and more vinegar. The soup should be savoury, slightly sharp, and just lightly sweet.
Remove the bay leaves. Stir in the dill. Rest for 10 minutes off the heat before serving.
Ladle into deep bowls. Top each portion with a spoonful of soured cream. Serve with dark rye bread.

items.symptom: The soup has turned brown rather than red.
items.cause: The vinegar was not added, or the soup boiled hard for too long.
items.fix: Add the vinegar as soon as possible and avoid boiling at full heat. A tablespoon of beetroot juice stirred in at the end also helps restore colour.

items.symptom: The beetroot still tastes raw and sharp.
items.cause: The soup was not simmered long enough after the beetroot was added.
items.fix: Continue simmering until the beetroot is completely soft with no bite remaining. This takes at least 25 minutes.

items.symptom: The soup tastes flat despite seasoning.
items.cause: The balance of sour, sweet, and salt is off.
items.fix: Add a pinch more sugar and another small splash of vinegar before adjusting salt. These three elements must work together in borscht.
